paras: The averted lynching of Bill Slaton took place near Lithia Springs, Georgia, on August 20, 1903, when a posse of citizens captured Slaton, a Black man accused of assaulting eighteen-year-old Emma Strickland, and threatened to lynch him. Wire reports credited the young woman's father, Isaac Strickland, with saving Slaton by pleading that the law take its course, and the sheriff later moved him to Atlanta because of rumors of a mob.

According to a report from Lithia Springs, Emma Strickland was the daughter of a farmer who lived about a mile and a half from the town. That report said she was walking early in the morning near a clump of woods by her home when a young man darted out and grabbed her by the arm, and that she defended herself, got away and ran screaming to the house. The New York wire version instead said she had been "brutally assaulted" in the public road and "dragged herself to her home."

Once the alarm was given, neighbors and friends of the family pursued the accused man and caught him, by one account within a short distance of the house and by another two miles from the scene. He was held near the Sweetwater Park Hotel to await the sheriff from Douglasville, and the papers reported that he confessed while in the posse's hands. The New-York Tribune said he "would have been lynched except for the protestations of his victim's father," while the Savannah Morning News's Lithia Springs item credited "the cooler heads."

Under heavy guard Slaton was delivered to the sheriff and lodged in the jail at Douglasville. Rumors then spread that a mob was forming there, and Sheriff Hatchcock of Douglas county, who was in Atlanta, took the first train back. He found no mob, but he took Slaton by carriage on a roundabout route to the railroad station at Fairburn and brought him to the Tower in Atlanta at midnight.
No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage, which ends within about a week of the capture.

The story reached the press through a telegraph dispatch dated Austell, which the New-York Tribune ran under the headline "Saves Negro from Mob" and The Sun printed with an "Austin, Ga." dateline on August 21. Shortened versions headed "Rapist Saved from Mob" appeared in the Gainesville Star and the Bamberg Herald, and the Newberry Herald and News carried a brief among its general news notes. A later wire, printed in North Dakota papers on August 28 as "Negro Ravisher Jailed," added a detailed account of a completed assault.

These reports treated the accusation and the reported confession as established and centered the father's plea for law and order. The Savannah Morning News, drawing on Georgia sources, described the charge as an attempted assault and gave most attention to the sheriff's precautions. No coverage of the case was found in the Black press.

The wire reports said the assault was completed, while both Savannah Morning News reports called it an attempt in which the young woman escaped. The Georgia accounts were sent from Lithia Springs and Atlanta, closer to the events than the wire. The Lithia Springs report also gave the accused man's name as "Bill Stratton," and one later wire printed the young woman's name as "Elma."

reader.title: Averted lynching of Bill Slaton
bases: A posse or 'mob' that captured Bill Slaton was reported ready to lynch him and was stopped by the accuser's father or 'cooler heads', and lynching rumors later led the sheriff to move him to Atlanta (A1, A2, A3, A4); no one was killed, so this is an averted lynching.

A posse of 'infuriated citizens' threatened to lynch Slaton on an accusation of assault, but every report says the lynching was prevented and he was delivered to the sheriff and later moved to the Atlanta Tower (A1, A2, A3, A4); no one was killed.

A New York wire (A1, A2) and Georgia-sourced reports in the Savannah Morning News (A3, A4) independently agree that Slaton was captured by pursuers, threatened with lynching, and turned over to the law, though they differ on whether the assault was completed.

accounts.label: Wire report (Austell / 'Austin' dateline)
accounts.gist: Slaton brutally assaulted the girl in the road, was captured by a posse, confessed, and was saved from lynching only by her father's pleas; he was jailed at Douglassville.

accounts.label: Lithia Springs report
accounts.gist: The man grabbed her arm but she got away and ran screaming home; neighbors caught him near the house and held him at the Sweetwater Park Hotel, where 'cooler heads' prevented a lynching.

accounts.label: Atlanta report
accounts.gist: Charged with attempted assault, Slaton was taken from the Douglasville jail to the Atlanta Tower at midnight because of lynching rumors, though the sheriff found no mob.

framing.detail: Northern and South Carolina papers headlined the case 'Saves Negro from Mob' and 'Rapist Saved from Mob', treating the accusation as fact while praising the father's plea for law and order.
The Savannah Morning News used 'Would-Be Ravisher' and reported the charge as an attempt, focusing on the sheriff's precautions.
Dakota papers ran the later wire as 'Negro Ravisher Jailed', describing a completed assault in detail.
